headline: Authorized a $300 fine for 461 Northampton Street; continued flood pump station and 500 Easthampton Road hearings.
summary: Work on seven flood pump stations would be done in phases as funding becomes available. Concrete washout in a wetland buffer at 98 Lower Westfield Road led to a requirement for three sensitive-area signs.
decisions: Continued the flood pump station Notice of Intent public hearing to October 22, 2026, by a 6-0 roll call vote.
Continued the Notice of Intent for 500 Easthampton Road to December 10, 2026, by a 6-0 roll call vote.
Required three sensitive-area signs at 98 Lower Westfield Road, approved 6-0 by roll call.
Continued the Enforcement Order for 98 Lower Westfield Road to November 12, 2026, by a 6-0 roll call vote.
Authorized a $300 fine notice to Nilsa Laboy for noncompliance at 461 Northampton Street, approved 6-0 by roll call.
Continued the Enforcement Order for 5 Appleton Street to October 22, 2026, by a 6-0 roll call vote.

decision_titles: Flood Pump Station Improvements Notice of Intent
Sensitive-area signs at 98 Lower Westfield Road
Enforcement Order for 98 Lower Westfield Road
plain_text:
Page 1 of 8 
 
Holyoke Conservation Commission Meeting Minutes 10/8/26 (Remote via 
Zoom) 
Conservation Commission Members Present: Jeffery Horan (Chairperson), Mary Moriarty 
(Vice Chairperson), Patricia Normand, John Perdrizet, Bernice Bowler, Rosemary Arnold 
Conservation Commission Members Absent: Michael Dodge 
Staff Present: Joseph Pellegrino, Sean Mullen 
Members of the Public and Other Representatives Present: Colin Powers (Tighe & 
Bond), Matt, Mike Gallagher (Department of Public Works), Peter Rosskothen, Ned 
Barowsky, Pete Maldonado, Nina Orellana. 
1. Call to Order 
Chairperson Horan called the meeting to order at 6:15pm. The recording began a few 
seconds after the call to order. 
2. Public Hearing – Notice of Intent – Flood Pump Station Improvements 
• Applicant: City of Holyoke Department of Public Works 
• Representative: Tighe & Bond 
• Location: Multiple Sites  
• Description: The proposed project includes electrical upgrades to the existing 
Flood Pump Stations #1 through #7, sluice gate actuator replacements at 
Tailrace Structure #6 and the Tailrace Intake and Gatehouse Structures #24, as 
well as limited building envelope repairs at Flood Pump Stations #5 through #7  
 
Colin Powers attended on behalf of Tighe & Bond and shared a map of the project 
locations. He explained that much of the flood control infrastructure dates to the 1930s 
and 1940s. The existing backup power system requires Holyoke Gas & Electric (HG&E) 
personnel to operate high-voltage equipment manually. The project would replace this 
system with 480-volt service to improve safety and reliability. Veolia maintains the 
stations, while HG&E provides electrical service. 
Mr. Powers stated that the project had been designed in two groups, Stations 1 through 
4 and Stations 5 through 7. Due to construction costs, the City intends to complete 
individual phases as funding becomes available. Station 2 is expected to be the first 
phase. The Notice of Intent (NOI) covers all seven stations and the gate structures so 
that later phases can proceed as funding is secured. 
Most work would occur inside the existing buildings. Existing electrical openings through 
the floodwall would be reused, with no new openings proposed. Exterior work includes 
underground electrical conduits, utility poles, and replacement transformer pads, 
generally within the existing pad footprints. Station 2 would have pole-mounted 
transformers because of space constraints. Stations 5, 6, and 7 would receive new 
doors and windows; Station 5 would receive a new roof; and Station 7 would require
Page 2 of 8 
 
exterior brick repointing. Existing pump motors would be rewound without changing 
station pumping capacity. Gate Structures 6 and 24 would receive motorized actuators 
to replace manual operation. 
Mr. Powers reported that a MassDEP file number had not yet been issued. He 
anticipated that the work would qualify for a Massachusetts Endangered Species Act 
exemption, but the relevant determinations and Natural Heritage review were still 
pending. A favorable determination had been received from the Massachusetts 
Historical Commission for all seven sites. 
Commissioner Perdrizet asked whether the work would remain within the existing 
buildings. Mr. Powers explained that the exterior conduits and transformer work would 
not expand the permanent surface disturbance beyond the existing developed areas. 
Vice Chairperson Moriarty asked about the schedule. Mr. Powers stated that 
construction funding for the first phase had been awarded through the Dam and 
Seawall Program, with the City still working to secure the required match. Bidding and 
construction could begin as early as spring 2027, subject to funding and preparation of 
phase-specific plans. Equipment lead times were estimated at three to six months. 
Vice Chairperson Moriarty requested a note on the construction plans requiring the 
contractor to contact the Conservation Agent before work begins. Mr. Powers agreed. 
She also requested an operations and maintenance plan. Mr. Powers stated that Tighe 
& Bond would coordinate with Veolia to ensure that its maintenance plan reflects the 
improvements. 
The Commission discussed the local variance request. Commissioner Bowler requested 
that the applicant complete the Commission’s variance form so that the relevant 
impacts, including temporary work within the 50-foot Buffer Zone, would be 
consolidated in one place. Chairperson Horan suggested attaching Table 4.1 from the 
application. Mr. Powers agreed to complete the form, and staff would provide it. 
The Commission discussed visiting representative stations before deciding on Limited 
Project status. Mr. Powers recommended Station 7 at Springdale Park because it is 
accessible and includes the greatest green-space disturbance. He also identified 
Stations 1 and 2 as accessible locations. In response to Chairperson Horan, Mr. Powers 
estimated that conduit trenches would be no more than approximately four feet deep 
and three feet wide, generally 20 feet or less in length, with the longest approximately 
50 feet. Excavated material was expected to be reused as backfill. New transformer 
pads would likely be precast and smaller than the existing pads. Gate controls would be 
located at the structures rather than remotely operated. 
Mr. Pellegrino confirmed receipt of the abutter notification documentation. Chairperson 
Horan invited public questions; none were raised. The Commission would coordinate a 
site visit after receiving an update on the pending agency reviews. Chairperson Horan 
stated that the site visit, Natural Heritage response, and MassDEP file number and 
comments were needed before the Commission could act on the NOI. No determination 
on Limited Project status or permit approval was made.
Page 3 of 8 
 
Commissioner Bowler motioned to continue the Public Hearing to 10/22/26. 
Commissioner Normand seconded the motion. The motion carried unanimously, 6-0, by 
roll call, with Commissioners Horan, Moriarty, Normand, Perdrizet, Bowler, and Arnold 
voting in favor. 
Introduction of Nina Orellana 
Mr. Pellegrino introduced Nina Orellana, a Holyoke resident interested in the 
Commission’s work. Ms. Orellana described her civil engineering background and 
interest in local projects. The Commissioners welcomed her engagement. 
 
3. Notice of Intent DEP WE# 186-0306 – Continued from 8/27/26  
• Applicant: Salmar Realty, Inc.  
• Representative: R. Levesque Associates  
• Location: 500 Easthampton Road (MBP: 213-00-003, 212-00-001)  
• Description: Commercial redevelopment within the Buffer Zone of Bordering 
Vegetated Wetlands  
 
Peter Rosskothen provided an update on the proposed protection of 5.7 acres 
associated with the project. He explained that habitat work would require identifying 
areas for tree cutting to allow additional light and moss growth for salamander habitat. 
The trees would be cut and left in place. Follow-up maintenance would be needed in 
approximately three to five years to keep the areas open. 
Mr. Rosskothen stated that the City of Easthampton remained interested in accepting 
the property but did not want to undertake the required maintenance work. He had 
proposed completing the initial tree cutting before transferring the property, with 
Easthampton assuming future maintenance. That arrangement had not been resolved. 
If Easthampton would not accept the property, the applicant would need to identify an 
organization willing to hold a conservation restriction and determine how the 
maintenance would be funded and performed. 
In response to Commissioner Arnold, Mr. Rosskothen identified GZA as the 
environmental consultant that would identify the cutting locations. A tree contractor had 
not yet been hired. He anticipated needing another two to three months to resolve the 
remaining issues, including Easthampton Conservation Commission and City Council 
review if the transfer proceeds. Construction in fall 2026 was no longer considered 
feasible, and the applicant hoped to begin in spring 2027. 
Commissioner Normand motioned to continue the Public Hearing to 12/10/26. 
Commissioner Arnold seconded the motion. The motion carried unanimously, 6-0, by 
roll call, with Commissioners Horan, Moriarty, Normand, Perdrizet, Bowler, and Arnold 
voting in favor.
Page 4 of 8 
 
4. Enforcement Order – 98 Lower Westfield Road 
• Description: Concrete washout disposal in the wetland buffer area near Tannery 
Brook. 
Mr. Pellegrino reported on his site visit earlier that day. Approximately 90 percent of the 
concrete had been removed with little apparent soil disturbance. Small pieces remained, 
including material partly covered by soil and material near the base of an autumn olive 
shrub. 
Property owner Ned Barowsky stated that sidewalk repairs had occurred on the 
property but that he had not known concrete was being discharged nearby. Pete 
Maldonado of Construction Services presented his company’s internal investigation and 
photographs. He stated that the driver had followed the contractor to a designated 
washout location and had washed residual concrete from the truck’s chutes. He 
distinguished this from emptying the drum, explaining that material and rinse water 
inside the drum had been returned to the plant. He acknowledged that the washout 
occurred in a buffer area but stated that the brook was not visible and that no signs 
identified the sensitive area. He also described annual environmental training for 
drivers. 
Vice Chairperson Moriarty asked who the contractor was. Mr. Maldonado identified 
Owens General Contractor. He initially understood that the contractor was performing 
work for Holyoke Water Works. Mr. Barowsky subsequently clarified that he had hired a 
contractor to repair a sidewalk patch on his property and had not authorized dumping. 
Commissioners Moriarty and Arnold questioned the practice of relying on a contractor’s 
direction without confirming that disposal was allowed at the location. Chairperson 
Horan discussed the importance of identifying appropriate concrete washout areas on 
project plans. 
Vice Chairperson Moriarty raised concerns about recurring litter in the area. Mr. 
Barowsky stated that litter from neighboring properties reaches his property and that he 
would arrange additional cleanup as needed. The Commission reviewed the 
Enforcement Order and questioned why cleanup had occurred despite its cease-and-
desist direction. Mr. Maldonado stated that his company had not removed the material. 
Mr. Barowsky stated that his property manager had reported the cleanup but that he 
did not know who had performed it. 
Mr. Pellegrino described two possible approaches: removal of the remaining concrete 
followed by consideration of a fine and closeout, or more extensive restoration involving 
erosion controls, invasive shrub removal, and native planting. Chairperson Horan 
questioned whether additional planting would be effective given the surrounding 
invasive vegetation and limited disturbance. Staff displayed the local fine schedule and 
recent photographs. The Commission discussed possible $50 and $300 fines, cleanup, 
and signage. 
Vice Chairperson Moriarty supported a fine as a deterrent. Commissioner Perdrizet 
questioned who should pay, noting that the contractor alleged to have directed the
Page 5 of 8 
 
washout was not present. Commissioners Bowler and Normand favored not fining Mr. 
Barowsky or Mr. Maldonado under the circumstances. Commissioner Arnold 
recommended cleanup and signs identifying the wetland as a sensitive area. Mr. 
Barowsky agreed to install signs, and Mr. Maldonado offered to pay for them. Staff 
displayed a parcel map to clarify the limited portion of the rear property owned by Mr. 
Barowsky. 
Commissioner Bowler motioned to require three sensitive-area signs along Mr. 
Barowsky’s approximately 70-foot rear property boundary at 20 to 25 foot intervals, 
behind the guardrail or fence, with Mr. Maldonado paying for the signs and Mr. 
Barowsky installing them and completing cleanup on his portion of the property. Staff 
would provide sign specifications and sourcing information. Commissioner Normand 
seconded the motion as clarified by Chairperson Horan. The motion carried 
unanimously, 6-0, by roll call, with Commissioners Horan, Moriarty, Normand, Perdrizet, 
Bowler, and Arnold voting in favor. 
Chairperson Horan stated that the Enforcement Order would remain open until the work 
was completed and inspected by staff. Mr. Pellegrino would connect Mr. Barowsky and 
Mr. Maldonado and provide guidance on sign wording, location, and installation. The 
Commission subsequently discussed wording identifying a wetland buffer or sensitive 
area and using existing signs at Gloutak Park as a reference. 
Vice Chairperson Moriarty motioned to continue the Enforcement Order to the first 
meeting in November, 11/12/26, to allow time to obtain and install the signs. 
Commissioner Normand seconded the motion. The motion carried unanimously, 6-0, by 
roll call, with Commissioners Horan, Moriarty, Normand, Perdrizet, Bowler, and Arnold 
voting in favor. 
Chairperson Horan stated that the parties would not need to return if the work was 
completed and verified by staff. The Commission also discussed contacting neighboring 
property owners to encourage similar signage. Chairperson Horan offered staff 
assistance with wetlands information for Mr. Maldonado’s driver training. 
5. Enforcement Order – 461 Northampton Street 
No representative of the property was present. Mr. Pellegrino reported sending a 
certified letter to the owner’s mailing address on 9/9/26, followed by certified and 
regular letters on 9/28/26 after the Commission’s 9/24/26 meeting. Staff had received 
no response. The discussion indicated that signed return receipts had not been 
received. 
The Commission reviewed the fine schedule. Members discussed the reported tree 
removal and wood chipping, prior enforcement matters, and the fact that staff had not 
been able to inspect the current work. The Commission focused on failure to comply 
with the Enforcement Order, identified as item G in the fine schedule, rather than 
imposing a fine based on unverified material disposal.
Page 6 of 8 
 
Mr. Mullen read the provision in the Holyoke Wetlands Regulations stating that each day 
or portion of a day during which a violation continues constitutes a separate offense, 
and that each provision violated constitutes a separate offense. The Commission 
discussed including that information in the notice, along with the $300 fine, payment 
instructions, the 21-day payment period, and possible consequences of continued 
noncompliance. Members also discussed potential collection measures for nonpayment. 
Chairperson Horan clarified that the property owner should attend the 11/12/26 
meeting regardless of whether the fine was paid. 
Vice Chairperson Moriarty motioned to authorize the Conservation Agent to send Nilsa 
Laboy a notice imposing a $300 fine for noncompliance with the Enforcement Order for 
461 Northampton Street. The notice would identify the applicable authority, explain the 
potential for additional fines for continued noncompliance, specify payment to the City 
of Holyoke within 21 days, and require attendance at the 11/12/26 meeting. 
Commissioner Bowler seconded the motion. The motion carried unanimously, 6-0, by 
roll call, with Commissioners Horan, Moriarty, Normand, Perdrizet, Bowler, and Arnold 
voting in favor. 
6. Enforcement Order – 5 Appleton Street 
Description: Grading and fill deposition along approximately 470 linear feet of the 
Connecticut River bank. 
Chairperson Horan stated that Randy Reynolds had been advised that he did not need 
to attend because staff was still awaiting MassDEP guidance. Mr. Pellegrino reported 
that the interim wetlands circuit rider had forwarded the soil analysis report to a 
MassDEP chemist for review, particularly regarding chrysotile asbestos. A response had 
not yet been received. Vice Chairperson Moriarty expressed concern about asbestos and 
other contaminants identified in the testing. The Commission did not reach a technical 
determination on the soil findings. 
Chairperson Horan expressed concern that the remaining growing season for 
establishing vegetation was limited. Mr. Pellegrino reported that, at his most recent 
inspection around the 9/24/26 meeting, the second silt fence was installed and the 
erosion controls appeared properly overlapped and staked. Members discussed whether 
the site could remain stabilized if restoration extended into spring and whether 
vegetation would establish in the existing material. 
Mr. Pellegrino stated that he had asked Sarah LaRose of HG&E for railroad contacts to 
help prevent further delays in obtaining coordination for restoration. Chairperson Horan 
emphasized that obtaining the necessary railroad response remained Mr. Reynolds’s 
responsibility, although staff outreach might assist. Staff and Commissioners attending 
a separate site visit with Ms. LaRose the following day could discuss those contacts. 
Commissioner Bowler motioned to continue the Enforcement Order to 10/22/26 while 
awaiting responses from MassDEP, Pinsly Railroad, and Natural Heritage concerning 
remediation. Commissioner Normand seconded the motion. The motion carried
Page 7 of 8 
 
unanimously, 6-0, by roll call, with Commissioners Horan, Moriarty, Normand, Perdrizet, 
Bowler, and Arnold voting in favor. 
7. Discussion – Commission Roles and Upcoming Vacancies 
Chairperson Horan reminded the Commission that he intended to step down from the 
Commission in January 2027. Members would need to consider the Chairperson and 
Vice Chairperson positions. Commissioner Normand confirmed that she had taken over 
the Commission’s CPA representative role from Vice Chairperson Moriarty. The 
Commission also discussed a request for a representative on the data center 
committee. Mr. Pellegrino stated that staff was exploring whether a staff member could 
serve in that role. 
Vice Chairperson Moriarty stated that she preferred another member to serve as 
Chairperson but would consider the position if no one else was available. Mr. Pellegrino 
encouraged members to begin considering the upcoming roles, noting that only three 
meetings remained in 2026 after that evening. 
8. Minutes from 8/13/26 Meeting 
Vice Chairperson Moriarty reported that she had reviewed the recording and sent 
corrections to the draft minutes. Mr. Pellegrino stated that the revisions had not been 
finalized for a vote at this meeting. No vote was taken on the 8/13/26 minutes. 
The Commission discussed staff’s preparation of minutes and agenda review materials. 
Chairperson Horan thanked staff for the detailed agenda review and encouraged Mr. 
Pellegrino and Mr. Mullen to develop a workable process and to decide on level of detail 
for future materials. Vice Chairperson Moriarty noted that automated transcripts still 
require careful review for inaccuracies. 
9. Discussion – Upcoming Items for 10/22/26 Meeting 
Mr. Pellegrino reported that an RDA had been submitted for a pavilion at the Holyoke 
Revolver Club. The project had initially been described as installing footings through an 
existing concrete slab. Subsequent discussions suggested that portions of the slab 
might be removed and excavated if rocks were encountered, potentially resulting in 
more disturbance within the 100-foot Buffer Zone. Staff displayed the submitted 
materials and discussed the uncertainty in the proposed construction method. 
Commissioner Bowler cautioned against further substantive discussion before the 
scheduled review, and the Commission deferred further consideration. No determination 
was made. 
Mr. Pellegrino also reported that the Department of Conservation and Recreation was 
considering an extension of the Order of Conditions for the Bray Lake Trail. Although 
closing out the permit had been discussed, he had advised seeking a one-year 
extension because of the proposed trail maintenance. Chairperson Horan supported 
discussing an extension, noting that the trail had not been built exactly as originally
Page 8 of 8 
 
designed. Commissioner Bowler stated that conditions had improved but that some 
issues remained. 
Mr. Pellegrino proposed site visits on Monday, 10/19/26, at 9:00 a.m. for the Bray Lake 
Trail and 10:30 a.m. for the Holyoke Revolver Club. He would follow up by email. 
Commissioner Bowler stated that she would be absent from the next Commission 
meeting. 
Mail/other items not reasonably anticipated by the Chair 
Vice Chairperson Moriarty renewed her offer to lead an approximately two-hour tour for 
staff and interested Commissioners. The group tentatively selected the morning of 
10/14/26, approximately 9:00 to 11:00 a.m. Chairperson Horan also invited Ms. 
Orellana to consider the anticipated Commission vacancy in January. Ms. Orellana 
expressed interest in continuing to attend meetings. 
Adjourn 
Meeting was adjourned at 8:39 p.m.  
Referenced documents 
Flood pump station NOI materials, location map, and plans, including Table 4.1; 98 
Lower Westfield Road Enforcement Order; Mr. Maldonado’s investigation presentation 
and photographs; staff photographs from the 10/8/26 site visit; Parcel map for 98 
Lower Westfield Road; Holyoke Wetlands Regulations and fine schedule; 5 Appleton 
Street soil analysis report discussed during the meeting; Draft 8/13/26 minutes and 
proposed corrections; Holyoke Revolver Club Site Plan.
